summary: Describes a way to try out new DNSSEC approaches that are not compatible with the standard ones, without disturbing normal DNSSEC deployment. It sets up a methodology for running such experiments in parallel. It is a standards-track document aimed at DNS security researchers.

eli5.summary: A way for scientists to test new locks on the internet's phone book without breaking the locks people already use.

questions: what are unknown dnssec algorithm identifiers
how do validators treat unknown ds algorithms
can a dnssec experiment break resolution
subtitle: A recipe for testing non-backwards-compatible DNSSEC ideas on real zones without breaking standard resolvers.

tldr.problem: Experiments with DNSSEC changes that are not backwards compatible can make a zone look bogus or broken to existing security-aware resolvers.
tldr.mechanism: Sign the experimental zone with only unknown algorithm identifiers, and publish only unknown identifiers in the parent's DS records. Standard validators then treat the zone as unsigned, while resolvers that know the experiment can validate it.
tldr.outcome: Experiments can coexist with standard DNSSEC. The cost is that a zone is either in an experiment or in a classic island of security, and unaware resolvers cannot build a chain of trust through it.

today: RFC 4955 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DNSSEC Experiments Are Hard
sections.content:
Experimenting with alternatives to DNSSEC has historically been a problem. People want to introduce non-backwards-compatible changes and also try them on real zones in the public DNS. But such a change can make all or part of a zone appear bogus or broken to existing security-aware resolvers.

This document describes a standard methodology for setting up DNSSEC experiments. It handles coexistence with standard DNSSEC and DNS by using unknown algorithm identifiers to hide the experimental modifications from standard security-aware resolvers. Familiarity with RFC 1035 and RFCs 4033, 4034 and 4035 is assumed.
sections.eli5: If you try a new kind of lock on a real door, everyone with an old key might think the door is broken. This RFC shows how to test the lock without upsetting them.

sections.title: Kinds of Experiments
sections.content:
The RFC splits experiments into two broad categories.

  • Backwards-compatible: changes that do not strictly follow the DNSSEC standard but still interoperate with clients and servers that implement it.
  • Non-backwards-compatible: changes that would make a standard security-aware resolver wrongly decide that all or part of a zone is bogus, or otherwise fail to interoperate.

Experiments with the core DNS protocol itself are not covered. The methodology is not necessary for backwards-compatible experiments, although it may be used if desired.
sections.eli5: Some changes are like a new coat of paint, and old keys still work. Others change the lock itself, and those are the ones that need special care.

sections.title: The Method: Unknown Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
The core of the method is to use strictly unknown algorithm identifiers when signing the experimental zone. More importantly, the DS records for the delegation at the parent contain only unknown algorithm identifiers.

This works because of what RFC 4035 Section 5.2 says validators do. If the validator supports none of the algorithms in an authenticated DS RRset, it has no supported authentication path to the child. It SHOULD treat the child zone as if it were unsigned. That is not a MUST, but the RFC argues a validator can only treat the responses as insecure or as bogus, and treating them as bogus would defeat the purpose of the rule. Local policy still lets a validator refuse to trust a zone for any reason.

Because these are experiments, the RFC RECOMMENDS private algorithm numbers (see RFC 4034, Appendix A.1.1). Rather than invent new algorithms, the recommended path is to make alternate identifiers that are aliases for existing algorithms. It is suggested that all optional defined algorithms be aliased too.

It is RECOMMENDED to pick a domain name base for the experiment and prepend the algorithm number to it. For example, with the base dnssec-experiment-a.example.com, algorithm 3 (DSA) becomes 3.dnssec-experiment-a.example.com and algorithm 5 (RSASHA1) becomes 5.dnssec-experiment-a.example.com. Any unique identifier will do.
sections.eli5: The experiment gives the old locks new secret nicknames. Old guards do not know the nicknames, so they just say they cannot check this door, instead of sounding the alarm.

sections.title: Defining an Experiment
sections.content:
An experiment MUST define the set of previously unknown algorithm identifiers that identify it, and what each one means. Unless the experiment really tests a new signing algorithm, this is a mapping of private identifiers to existing known algorithms.

Normally the experiment picks a DNS name as the identifier base, which SHOULD be under the control of the experiment's authors. It may instead use the Object Identifier (OID) private algorithm space with algorithm number 254, or use non-private algorithm numbers, which would require an IANA allocation.

Resolvers MUST only recognize the experiment's semantics when present in a zone signed by one or more of its algorithm identifiers. This isolates one experiment from others the resolver might understand. Resolvers in the experiment are generally expected to understand both standard DNSSEC and the experimental protocol, though that is not required.

The method creates two classes of security-aware servers and resolvers: those aware of the experiment and those unaware of it. It also means a zone cannot be both in an experiment and in a classic island of security.
sections.eli5: Every experiment must publish its own list of nicknames and say what each one means, so people who join in know the rules.

sections.title: Considerations and Non-Experiments
sections.content:
The RFC lists two caveats. If an unaware validator does not follow the rules of RFC 4035, for example by interpreting a DNSSEC record before validating it, or if the experiment reaches beyond DNSSEC semantics, the experiment may not be masked well enough and could cause unintended resolution failures. Also, security-aware resolvers unaware of the experiment cannot build a chain of trust through an experimental zone.

The method MAY also be used for non-backwards-compatible DNSSEC changes that start out as, or become, standards. Then the change SHOULD use public IANA-allocated algorithm identifiers instead of private ones, which helps mark it as a standard rather than an experiment. Resolvers MAY recognize the change in zones not signed, or not solely signed, with the new identifiers.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a guard who ignores the rules may still be confused, and nobody outside the experiment can vouch for the door. Real, permanent changes should use official nicknames.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Zones using this method are considered insecure by all resolvers except those aware of the experiment. It is generally not possible to create a secure delegation from an experimental zone that unaware resolvers will follow.

Implementers should consider the risks of environments configured to trust both experimental and non-experimental zones. If an experimental zone is more vulnerable to attack, it could be used to promote trust in zones outside the experiment, possibly under an attacker's control.
sections.eli5: If the test door has a weak lock and you trust it like the others, a bad guy could use it to sneak in a fake door.
